ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Judgments nevertheless improved more when participants had selected sources, particularly when those sources were initially accurate.

> At the same time, judgments improved more when participants had selected sources to observe, and selected-source accuracy was positively associated with improvement.

> Our participants instead chose sources without access to their opinions or accuracy, and networks and identifiers were reset between headlines.

> Participants were recruited through Prolific, were residents of the United States, and had an approval rate above 80%.

> They provided informed consent and received a base payment of £6 plus performance-dependent compensation.

> In Phase 3 (75 s), the final network was fixed and participants completed five 15-s updates, observing at each period their selected sources' previous reports.

> Participants were informed that the private report and the final report in the fifth Phase 3 period contributed to performance-based compensation.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study was approved by the GATE-Lab Review Board for ethical standards in research (GATE, UMR 5824, CNRS; project 2024-01 and approved extension 2024-01bis).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). Note: this percentage counts only `#` comments; 3 of these Python files are documented via docstrings (`"""..."""`), which are not counted as comments here since they are string literals, not comment syntax.

#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 277 files: 88 data, 6 code, 97 documentation, 84 materials, 2 output.
-  We found 88 tabular data files and extracted 1117 columns from 84 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex1), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
-  2 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass `local_path` to point at a local copy.

No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: analysis_environment.csv, Table_S9_archived_software_environment.csv. We ran automated data-quality checks on 1117 columns; 10 columns have at least one potential issue (4 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 3 columns with numeric values stored as text; 2 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 1 column whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1117 columns across 84 data files.
#### Issues Identified

10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 84 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments.
We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy.
Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates.

During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden.
Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection.
Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources.
Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure.
Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy.
Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty.
Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update.

These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.
Before people learn from others, they choose whom to observe.
We studied this choice in groups evaluating true and false news.
Displaying how certain other people appeared attracted links toward more certain individuals, even before their opinions were revealed.
The resulting networks were denser, but selected sources were not clearly more accurate, and visibility produced no detectable average accuracy benefit.
Under the experimental cost structure, reconstructed net scores were lower.
Judgments nevertheless improved more when participants had selected sources, particularly when those sources were initially accurate.
These results show why the cues that organize attention matter for collective judgment: attracting observers and providing useful information are different properties of a source.
People rarely evaluate uncertain information in isolation.
They encounter others' judgments, decide whose views deserve consideration, and revise their beliefs in response.
Social influence can improve judgment by pooling dispersed information, but it can also amplify errors and reduce the diversity on which collective accuracy depends [1] [2] [3] [4].
text.formatted: Social influence can improve judgment by pooling dispersed information, but it can also amplify errors and reduce the diversity on which collective accuracy depends <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Understanding these outcomes requires explaining two connected processes: how people select their sources and how they integrate the information those sources provide.
Formal models such as DeGroot learning and bounded-confidence models describe how beliefs propagate through a specified network [5] [6] [7].
text.formatted: Formal models such as DeGroot learning and bounded-confidence models describe how beliefs propagate through a specified network <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Network structure determines which judgments become available and how unevenly influence is distributed.
Experiments show that decentralized networks can support collective accuracy, while concentrated influence makes outcomes more dependent on particular individuals [3, 8].
text.formatted: Experiments show that decentralized networks can support collective accuracy, while concentrated influence makes outcomes more dependent on particular individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Networks can also adapt: when people receive reliable performance feedback, they can redirect links toward more accurate sources [9].
text.formatted: Networks can also adapt: when people receive reliable performance feedback, they can redirect links toward more accurate sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Yet source selection often occurs without such feedback, sometimes before a source's opinion is even known.
In these settings, the value of network adaptation depends on what the available cues reveal about potential sources.
Two cues may be particularly influential.
Popularity can attract attention without directly establishing source quality [10, 11].
text.formatted: Popularity can attract attention without directly establishing source quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Expressed confidence can also shape perceived competence, advice seeking, trust, and interpersonal influence [12] [13] [14] [15] [16].
text.formatted: Expressed confidence can also shape perceived competence, advice seeking, trust, and interpersonal influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Previous work has examined how confidence affects the weighting of opinions after they become available [16] [17] [18].
text.formatted: Previous work has examined how confidence affects the weighting of opinions after they become available <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: A related question concerns an earlier stage: does appearing certain determine whether someone's opinion becomes available for observation in the first place?
Because highly certain judgments can be either correct or incorrect, a cue that attracts observers need not direct them toward useful information.
We examined this source-selection process in an online experiment in which participants constructed their own news-veracity observation networks.
Across eight sessions, 273 participants contributed judgments about the same 14 headlines.
For each headline, they first reported a private belief, then selected sources through costly directed links, and finally revised their beliefs while observing those sources.
We manipulated whether potential sources' judgment certainty was displayed during network formation.
This direction-free cue was derived from the extremity of the private probability report, rather than elicited as an independent metacognitive confidence judgment.
The evolving network remained visible in both conditions, making current popularity observable, but sources' belief direction and actual accuracy were unavailable while links were chosen.
Only selected sources' beliefs became visible during updating; truth feedback was not supplied.
This design separates certainty-guided selection from selection based on known agreement or demonstrated performance.
The experiment also differs from news-judgment studies in which unconnected individuals see predetermined popularity, endorsement, or source cues [19] [20] [21] [22] [23].
text.formatted: The experiment also differs from news-judgment studies in which unconnected individuals see predetermined popularity, endorsement, or source cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Here, participants' choices created the network through which information subsequently propagated.
It complements work on how confidence in one's own news judgment guides information demand [24] by asking how another person's displayed certainty guides the choice of source.
text.formatted: It complements work on how confidence in one's own news judgment guides information demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> by asking how another person's displayed certainty guides the choice of source.

text.text: Resetting networks and participant identifiers between headlines further limited the development of stable source reputations.
Our questions were therefore how displayed certainty changes whom people choose to observe, and what consequences those choices have for subsequent judgments.
We first characterize private judgments, then network formation and selected-source quality, and finally accuracy, information costs, and belief updating.
The central result is a dissociation: displaying certainty reorganized source selection and increased network density without a detectable average accuracy benefit.
Source quality was associated with improvement within the networks participants formed, while compact updating models captured some, but not all, of the subsequent belief dynamics.
These analyses distinguish a randomized change in the information available for source selection from the observational consequences of the sources participants chose.

For each headline, participants reported a private probability judgment on a 0-100 scale (Phase 1, 30 s), constructed a directed observation network (Phase 2, 60 s), and completed five successive belief updates (Phase 3, five 15-s periods; Fig. 1).

text.text: Displaying judgment certainty changed the information environments participants constructed.
It increased network density, redirected source selection toward more certain individuals, and increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments.
These changes did not produce a detectable average accuracy benefit.
Under the task's payoff structure, reconstructed net scores were lower.
At the same time, judgments improved more when participants had selected sources to observe, and selected-source accuracy was positively associated with improvement.
Together, the findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify information that improves judgment.
This distinction places source selection alongside information integration as a determinant of collective belief formation.
Previous experiments show that network plasticity can improve collective accuracy when performance feedback helps participants identify better sources [9].
text.formatted: Previous experiments show that network plasticity can improve collective accuracy when performance feedback helps participants identify better sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Our participants instead chose sources without access to their opinions or accuracy, and networks and identifiers were reset between headlines.
Popularity provided a dynamic social cue, while visible certainty created an additional basis for selection.
The resulting shift toward certainty was much clearer than the shift toward accuracy.
This does not mean that certainty was wholly unrelated to correctness; rather, displaying it did not reliably improve the relative accuracy of the sources selected.
The experiment therefore identifies the information available for choosing sources as an important condition on the value of network adaptation.
The results extend research on confidence in social learning to the stage at which information becomes available.
Confidence can affect advice seeking, trust, and the weighting of opinions after they have been exchanged [15] [16] [17].
text.formatted: Confidence can affect advice seeking, trust, and the weighting of opinions after they have been exchanged <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Here, another person's displayed certainty affected whether that person's judgment entered the observer's information environment at all.
Unlike predetermined endorsement or popularity cues attached to a news item [10, 11, 22], these choices jointly constructed a network through which beliefs could propagate.
text.formatted: Unlike predetermined endorsement or popularity cues attached to a news item <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>, these choices jointly constructed a network through which beliefs could propagate.

text.text: Because belief direction was hidden during linking, the certainty-directed choices cannot be explained by known agreement with the source.
What participants encountered was associated with what they subsequently learned.
Selectedsource accuracy predicted improvement across sessions and alternative definitions of highly connected sources.
This complements work on identifying and weighting expertise [25]: in a self-formed network, informative judgments must first be selected before they can influence anyone.
text.formatted: This complements work on identifying and weighting expertise <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>: in a self-formed network, informative judgments must first be selected before they can influence anyone.

text.text: It also accords with models in which the value of communication depends on evidence quality and source evaluation [26, 27].
text.formatted: It also accords with models in which the value of communication depends on evidence quality and source evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27]</ref>.

text.text: These relationships characterize self-selected exposure rather than a randomized effect of source quality.

Similarly, the finding that more certain participants revised less does not establish that more accurate participants revised less, the revision pattern implicated in some accounts of decentralized collective accuracy [3, 8].
text.formatted: Similarly, the finding that more certain participants revised less does not establish that more accurate participants revised less, the revision pattern implicated in some accounts of decentralized collective accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: The computational analyses describe the subsequent integration stage.
Ordinary averaging captured movement toward selected sources but predicted too much compression toward uncertainty.
A modest certainty-reinforcement transformation improved penalized and held-out prediction, without requiring strong certainty-based source weighting.
The improvement was incremental, and all tested compact averaging models missed the large initial response to newly revealed beliefs.
Agreement also did not uniformly produce extremization in the behavioral data.

These observations support certainty reinforcement as a compact predictive description while leaving open whether the remaining discrepancy reflects asymmetric responses to agreement and disagreement, private reconsideration, or heterogeneous first-exposure responses.
First-exposure dynamics therefore remain unresolved; the model preference does not establish a unique individual updating mechanism.
The score findings add an economic consequence to the selection-accuracy distinction.
Visible certainty encouraged greater expenditure on social information without a detectable compensating increase in final gross performance.
This treatment comparison should not be read as showing that every selected link was unhelpful: linked observations improved more, but the decision to link was not randomized.
Nor does a task-score difference establish a general welfare loss on online platforms, where attention costs, persistent identities, reputations, and quality signals differ.
The broader implication is that increased connectivity should be evaluated together with information quality and the cost of acquiring it, rather than taken as an improvement in itself.

High-certainty inaccurate sources may be especially consequential where cue validity is weaker or exposure more concentrated, but those possibilities remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated effects here [23, 28].
text.formatted: High-certainty inaccurate sources may be especially consequential where cue validity is weaker or exposure more concentrated, but those possibilities remain hypotheses rather than demonstrated effects here <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: The design also sets the scope of inference.
Randomization across eight sessions supports the reported treatment comparisons but limits their precision; a non-significant accuracy contrast is not evidence of equivalence.
Repetition of the same 14 headlines, only three headline sequences, and the resetting of networks constrain generalization to persistent information environments.
Certainty was derived from belief extremity, so the experiment concerns this observable cue rather than an independently measured metacognitive judgment.
Finally, participants without retained links could reconsider their answers or obtain information outside the experimental network.
The positive associations between exposure, source quality, and improvement should be interpreted within these boundaries.
Collective judgment is shaped before beliefs are revised.
By changing whom people choose to observe, a direction-free certainty cue can reorganize costly information acquisition without detectably improving average accuracy.
The value of self-formed networks therefore depends not only on their connectivity or updating rules, but also on whether the cues governing source selection make informative judgments accessible.

The experiment comprised eight online group sessions, four assigned to visible certainty and four to hidden certainty.
Session records identified 286 entrants.
Of these, 273 generated behavioral data and 239 completed all five updates for all 14 headlines.
The 47 participants who did not meet this strict complete-case definition comprised 13 with no main-task record and 34 with incomplete trials.

The own-certainty interaction was also checked separately in each session and under leave-one-session-out refitting.
Computational models were fitted to participant-headline observations with at least one retained outgoing link.
Simulations were recursive and synchronous on the fixed final network.
The analysis comprised 9,128 participant-headline-update observations across five updates and 1,823 final-step observations.
Models were fitted to individual observations, not to the mean trajectories plotted for visualization.
The no-update benchmark assumed b i,t+1 = b i,t = b i,0 .
Simple DeGroot computed with fitted social-update rate λ.

When S i (t) was non-empty, the participant updated toward the ordinary mean of accepted sources; otherwise the belief remained unchanged.

Certainty-reinforcing DeGroot first applied ordinary DeGroot mixing, p i,t = m i,t /100, then predicted b i,t+1 = 100 p β i,t where β = 1 recovers ordinary DeGroot and β > 1 increases the distance of interior beliefs from 50 while preserving direction and exact endpoints.

Across 3,504 participant-headline observations with both reports, mean accuracy rose from 64.42 at Phase 1 to 73.04 at the final Phase 3 judgment.

The secondary Phase-by-Visibility analysis estimated an 8.62-point Phase effect (p < .001), no clear average visibility effect (p = .527), and no Phase-by-Visibility interaction (p = .476; Supplementary Table S6).

text.text: The interaction conclusion agrees with the primary session-level visible-minus-hidden improvement contrast of -1.43 points (exact p = .943).

The resulting Phase 3 net scores were 42.12 and 24.73 (visible-minus-hidden difference -17.39, exact p = .029).
Linked observations improved by 12.43 accuracy points on average, compared with 4.50 points among observations with no retained source.

The linked-minus-zero-link difference was positive in all eight sessions (exact sign-flip p = .008); after adjustment for private accuracy, certainty, headline identity, and order, the difference was 6.44 points (SE = 1.05, p < .001; Supplementary Table S7).

All eight session-specific source-accuracy coefficients were positive (exact sign-flip p = .008).
The response to a fixed disagreement with selected sources decreased with participants' own certainty (Supplementary Fig. S4A).

text.text: In hidden-certainty networks, a 10-point disagreement predicted a 2.50-point revision at own certainty 0 and a 1.52-point revision at certainty 100.

The disagreement-by-own-certainty interaction was -0.098 response points per 10 certainty points (p = .002), was negative in all eight session-specific fits (exact sign-flip p = .008), and remained negative in every leave-one-session-out refit.
Moderation by source certainty (p = .097) and visibility (p = .165) was less conclusive.
Belief movement was strongly front-loaded.
The first update averaged 12.56 points for false news and 14.60 points for true news, and accounted for 44.0% of total absolute movement.
Simple, certainty-weighted, and certainty-reinforcing DeGroot predicted first-step movement of only about 4.7-4.9 points (Supplementary Fig. S4B,C).

text.text: Its BIC was 5.4 points lower than the hybrid, 209.4 lower than certainty-weighted DeGroot, 277.3 lower than simple DeGroot, and 286.4 lower than bounded-confidence DeGroot.
Aggregate leave-one-session-out and leave-one-item-out errors likewise favored certainty-reinforcing DeGroot among the compact models, with the hybrid very close (Supplementary Table S9).

text.text: Ordinary DeGroot compressed final beliefs too strongly toward 50.

At the final update, observed mean certainty was 79.85 for false news and 75.68 for true news; simple DeGroot predicted 48.29 and 41.73, whereas certainty-reinforcing DeGroot predicted 59.65 and 54.41.
Even the preferred compact model therefore left substantial discrepancies.

Behavioral checks also showed Supplementary Information that agreement did not uniformly induce extremization: when agreeing sources were less extreme than the participant, mean movement was 1.60 points toward moderation.
Certainty reinforcement should therefore be interpreted as a compact population-level predictive correction, not as a universal individual rule.

Experimental design.For each headline, participants first reported the probability that the headline was true (Phase 1, 30 s), then constructed a directed observation network by creating or deleting up to five costly links (Phase 2, 60 s), and finally revised their judgment over five consecutive 15-s update periods (Phase 3, 75 s total).
The lower sequence illustrates the evolution of the network during Phase 2.
The schematic shows the visible-certainty interface; hidden-certainty sessions were identical except that other participants' certainty labels were not displayed during network formation.
Belief direction remained hidden while links were chosen, and selected sources' numerical beliefs became visible only after the network was fixed.
The participant-facing label "level of confidence" denotes the computed certainty quantity in Eq. 1, not a separately elicited report.
Links cost 20 score points per retained source.
The example shown here gives 28 points if the headline is true and 68 points if it is false before link costs, and -12 and 28 points, respectively, after two retained links.
Only the Phase 1 and final Phase 3 reports were directly payoff-relevant.
